doc.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Re-recording 'Harlem Lullaby' for Horst Weber at Enja
summary: Rowe plays 'Harlem Lullaby'; Mance has just re-recorded it, with the Enja producer insisting on first takes.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Okay you probably know that I was going to play this next little piece, somewhere in here. This has some significance for me.
Is there a story behind this piece? The way you sat down —

No. Not really. I didn’t know what to call it, and then “Harlem Lullaby” stuck. But believe it or not I just recorded it again and I did it on this live session. And the producer liked it so well that I just did a record for them a few months ago. It should be out either this month or next month. And he asked me would I do it again for the session, I mean in the studio, and I did it. And I would have to send you that one because you know after you’ve done a tune a lot, then sometimes it either gets better or worse. Because sometimes you can get tired of doing it. I think I did the best one I ever did on this last

session. For one thing, recording for Enja, this particular producer I had, Horst Weber out of Munich, he insists on any, even in the studio, it’s almost like doing a live date because he will only use first takes. And just by coincidence he has the same idea about recording, which is, when you’ve got to do two or three takes, and I’ve always had this idea, if I have to repeat a thing, it goes downhill. Usually the first take, you’ve got the feeling that you want. You may miss a few notes. Horst doesn’t care. He says that’s jazz, everybody misses notes in jazz. It’s just that some of the older players, some of us know how to cover up. You know, we make a mistake, we make it sound right. And I don’t know I just felt pretty good. We did the session at night, myself and Earl May and Jackie Williams. And Earl and Jackie played a tune with me before. That’s usually the trio I use most of the time now except on the Floating Jazz Festival trios, Keter Betts is the bass player because he was sort of like the house bass player after Major Holley died. In fact we were put together as a trio on the cruise sort of by accident. And it was on the Royal Caribbean line too, it was a tribute to Benny Carter cruise, and the three of us played and we accompanied Benny and did nights by ourselves. And I don’t know it sort of just clicked. And at the end of the cruise Hank O’Neal, the producer of the group, he says, “Listen, can I record you guys in the studio?” I says, “Sure.” Hell we thought it would be down the line, but the next day he says, “We’re going to record at Rudy Van Gelder’s.” “Oh?” He says, “Can you be ready this afternoon?” And we were. That’s when we did this album called “Blue Mance.”
